To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
plant performance was greater in soils from more distantly related plant species for an herbaceous species in an old-field community.
the performance of a focal herb, Aquilegia canandensis, was greater in the soil of more distantly-related heterospecific plants than in the soil of less distantly-related hetero-specific plants.
the performance of an herbaceous understo-ry species was greater in the soil of more distantly-related plants, and this was due to soil legacy effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the potential role of soil legacy effects in the maintenance of plant species diversity, and our results suggest that soil legacy effects are an important mechanism for the coexistence of phytophagous species in plant communities.

the role of phylogenetic distance in the soil legacy effect, and we found evidence that the phylogenetic distance between plants may affect their performance through soil legacy effects in the absence of competition.
the potential for plant–plant competition and plant community assembly to be influenced by phylogenetic related-ness between species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the performance of A. candensis was greater in the soil of more distantly than less distantly related plants, but the mechanism underlying this result is unclear.
the performance of A. candensis is affected by phylogenetic distance of its neighbours.
the degree of relatedness between species influences the performance of A. candensis through soil legacy effects, and that this effect disappears with soil sterilization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
soil legacy effects can influence the outcome of competition between phylogenetically related species, and that these effects may be particularly strong for species that are susceptible to pathogens.
the degree of phylogenetically relatedness of a plant to its neighbours may be an important determinant of its performance in the understory, and thus of its coexistence with other species.
phylogeny can influence the outcome of competition through the soil legacy effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the degree of phylogenetically-relatedness between species may affect plant–soil feedbacks, which in turn may affect plant performance and community structure.
soil legacies can affect plant performance, and this may be particularly true for understory species.
the phylogenetic distance between plants may influence their interactions, even when they do not co-occur in nature.
